lead: An emission standard is a legal upper limit on what a vehicle may emit per kilometre of a fixed driving cycle: a mass in g/km for carbon monoxide (CO), hydrocarbons (HC), nitrogen oxides (NOx) and particulate matter (PM), and a count per km for particle number (PN). The limits exist because these gases and particles harm health and air. Each new stage lowers the ceilings, and India follows the European (Euro) ladder under the name Bharat Stage (BS). The tighter the ceiling, the more exactly the engine must meter fuel and time the spark, which is why the rest of this unit is about electronic control.
prereq: You need: the idea of rich and lean mixtures from engine fuelling and exhaust emissions. The lambda sensor itself is covered under Exhaust gas oxygen (lambda) sensors.

sections.h3: Limits per kilometre, for the whole vehicle

blocks.text: The regulated pollutants are CO, HC, NOx, PM and PN. CO is poisonous. HC and NOx form smog in sunlight. PM and PN are fine particles that reach deep into the lungs. A car limit is written in g/km: grams of that pollutant emitted for each kilometre driven. PN is written as particles per km.

The test runs the complete vehicle on a fixed driving cycle on a chassis dynamometer (rollers under the driven wheels), with the exhaust collected and analysed. So the result includes the engine, the catalyst and the gearing: it is a vehicle limit, not an engine limit. Heavy-duty engines are approved on an engine dynamometer instead, and their limits are in g/kWh of engine work. The two units cannot be compared.

A vehicle passes only if every pollutant is at or below its own ceiling. One failure fails the vehicle, however good the others are. Some diesel limits are written as a combined HC + NOx figure: add the two measured values before you compare.

All values are in g/km. BS VI also limits PN to 6 × 10¹¹ particles per km for diesels and direct-injection petrol cars. Notice the two big cuts from BS IV to BS VI: petrol NOx by 25 percent and diesel NOx by 68 percent.

sections.h3: The Euro ladder and the Bharat Stage steps

blocks.text: Euro 1 to Euro 6 is a ladder: each stage lowers the ceilings. India based Bharat Stage I to BS VI on that ladder, with its own driving cycle and dates. BS IV applied across the country from April 2017. India then skipped BS V and moved straight to BS VI in April 2020. With that change, the sulphur limit in petrol and diesel fell from 50 ppm (parts per million) to 10 ppm. Low sulphur keeps the catalyst active and lets a diesel particulate filter regenerate cleanly. A second BS VI phase from April 2023 added on-road (real driving) emission checks and stricter on-board diagnostics.
A stage is a type-approval limit for a vehicle family, not a quality mark on one engine. Homologation is the official approval test that a new model must pass before it can be sold.

What each step demands from the engine is the link to the rest of this unit. A petrol engine meets the limits with a three-way catalyst, which works only when the electronic control unit (ECU) holds the mixture at λ = 1, the chemically correct air-fuel ratio. That needs closed-loop electronic fuel control and precise spark timing, both run by the ECU (see concept of electronic engine control). A diesel runs lean (λ well above 1), so it cannot use a three-way catalyst; it cuts NOx with exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) and selective catalytic reduction (SCR), and traps soot in a particulate filter. Some syllabi call this topic emission legislation. Only a few universities teach it in depth.

examples.question: A petrol car on the test cycle emits 0.82 g/km CO, 0.07 g/km HC and 0.11 g/km NOx. Use the petrol limits in the table: BS IV CO 1.0, HC 0.10, NOx 0.08 g/km; BS VI CO 1.0, HC 0.10, NOx 0.06 g/km. (a) Express each result as a percentage of its limit. (b) Does the car pass BS IV? BS VI? (c) By how much must NOx fall to pass BS VI?
steps: CO: 0.82 ÷ 1.0 × 100 = 82 % of the limit under both stages. HC: 0.07 ÷ 0.10 × 100 = 70 % under both.
NOx against BS IV: 0.11 ÷ 0.08 × 100 = 137.5 % of the limit, that is 0.03 g/km (37.5 %) over.
NOx against BS VI: 0.11 ÷ 0.06 × 100 = 183.3 % of the limit, that is 0.05 g/km (83.3 %) over.
Pass needs every pollutant at or below 100 %. CO and HC pass, NOx fails, so the car fails both BS IV and BS VI.
To pass BS VI, NOx must fall from 0.11 to 0.06 g/km: a cut of 0.05 g/km, which is 0.05 ÷ 0.11 × 100 = 45.5 % of the present NOx.
examples.answer: CO is at 82 % and HC at 70 % of their limits, but NOx is at 137.5 % of the BS IV limit and 183.3 % of the BS VI limit, so the car fails both stages. NOx must fall by 0.05 g/km (45.5 %) to pass BS VI.

traps: Mixing units: g/km is a vehicle limit from a chassis dynamometer; g/kWh is an engine limit from an engine test.
Comparing HC and NOx separately when the stage gives a combined HC + NOx limit: add them first.
Writing that BS VI followed BS V. India skipped BS V and went from BS IV (2017) to BS VI (April 2020).
Treating PM and PN as the same. PM is a mass in g/km; PN is a count of particles per km.
Calling a vehicle a pass because most pollutants pass. One pollutant over its ceiling fails the vehicle.

quiz.q: Name the five regulated pollutants. Which one is counted as a number, not a mass?
quiz.a: CO, HC, NOx, PM and PN. PN (particle number) is a count per km.

quiz.q: Why is a g/km limit called a vehicle limit?
quiz.a: It is measured on the complete vehicle driven over a fixed cycle on a chassis dynamometer, so the engine, the catalyst and the gearing all affect the result.

quiz.q: The CO limit is 1.0 g/km and a car emits 0.85 g/km. What percentage of the limit is it, and what is the margin?
quiz.a: 0.85 ÷ 1.0 × 100 = 85 % of the limit; margin 0.15 g/km, or 15 %.

quiz.q: A car meets its CO and HC limits but its NOx is over. Does it pass the stage? Why?
quiz.a: No. A stage sets a separate ceiling for every pollutant and the vehicle must be at or below each one.

quiz.q: The NOx limit is 0.08 g/km and a car emits 0.09 g/km. Find the exceedance in g/km and percent.
Why can a g/km figure and a g/kWh figure not be compared?
quiz.a: g/km is grams of pollutant per kilometre driven by a whole vehicle on a driving cycle; g/kWh is grams per kilowatt-hour of work from an engine on a test bed. The bases are different.

quiz.q: A BS VI diesel car has HC 0.07 g/km and NOx 0.11 g/km. The limits are HC + NOx 0.17 and NOx 0.08 g/km. Does it pass?
quiz.a: HC + NOx = 0.18 g/km, over 0.17 by 0.01 g/km; NOx alone, 0.11 g/km, is also over 0.08. It fails on both counts.

beyond: Not for the exam. Calibration engineers trade NOx against fuel economy and cost while meeting a stage. Newer test procedures (the worldwide WLTC cycle and real driving emission tests with portable analysers) measure the car on real roads as well as on rollers. Research looks at very small particles below 23 nm and at life-cycle CO₂, which counts the power station behind an electric car. Search next for "Bharat Stage VI phase 2", "WLTC driving cycle" and "particle number limit".
